note.explanation: Newton’s laws explain how forces affect motion. The first law describes how an object resists a change in its motion, the second law links force to mass and acceleration, and the third law says forces between two interacting bodies are equal and opposite.
examples: When a bus stops suddenly, passengers tend to move forward because their bodies tend to keep moving.
When a gun fires a bullet forward, the gun recoils backward.
note.checkAnswer: The forces are equal and opposite, but they act on different bodies, so they do not balance each other.
note.simple: A force can change motion. Objects resist changes to their motion, and when two objects interact, each pushes or pulls the other.
note.checkQuestion: Why do action and reaction forces not balance each other?
note.title: Newton’s Laws of Motion
steps: Use the first law to describe what happens when no net external force acts.
Use F = ma when a question gives mass and acceleration, or asks for force.
For the third law, identify the two interacting bodies and state the equal, opposite forces acting on them.
note.answer: Newton’s first law describes inertia; the second law is F = ma; the third law says that every action has an equal and opposite reaction.

rationales: This is correct: without an external force changing its state, the book remains at rest.
Mass does not make an object speed up by itself; a net force is needed for acceleration.
The table supports the book, but that force does not push it forward.

rationales: This is correct: their bodies tend to maintain their state of motion because of inertia.
The passengers’ bodies tend to continue forward, not backward.
Passengers still have inertia because they have mass.
An upward force from the road does not explain the forward movement.

written.text: What kind of changes in motion may be produced by a force?
written.finalAnswer: A force may change the magnitude of velocity, its direction, or both.

rubric.how: State that the magnitude of velocity, or speed, may change.

written.text: An object moves with constant velocity in free space. How long will the object continue to move with this velocity?
written.finalAnswer: It will continue forever with constant velocity, provided no force acts on it.

rubric.why: The first law predicts continued uniform motion in the absence of an external force.
rubric.description: States that the motion continues without an end.
rubric.how: Answer that it continues forever or indefinitely.

rubric.why: The unchanged motion depends on there being no force to change it.
rubric.description: Links the continued motion to the absence of a force.
rubric.how: Mention that no force acts on the object.

modelAnswer: In free space, no force acts on the object.
According to Newton’s first law, it continues with constant velocity forever.
Final answer: It will continue forever with constant velocity, provided no force acts on it.

written.text: Why has not Newton's first law been proved on the Earth?
written.finalAnswer: Because friction acts on moving bodies on the Earth and changes their motion.

rubric.why: Friction is an external opposing force present in ordinary motion on Earth.
rubric.description: Identifies friction as the relevant force.
rubric.how: Name friction.

rubric.why: Friction prevents observing motion that remains unchanged with no force acting.
rubric.description: Explains how friction affects the body's motion.
rubric.how: Explain that friction slows or stops moving bodies.

modelAnswer: On the Earth, friction acts on moving bodies.
This opposing force changes their motion and eventually brings them to rest.
Final answer: Newton’s first law cannot be proved directly on the Earth because friction acts on moving bodies and changes their motion.

written.text: When sitting in a car which suddenly accelerates from rest, you are pushed back into the seat, why?
written.finalAnswer: Because of inertia, the body tends to maintain its state of rest as the car starts moving forward.

rubric.why: Inertia is the body's tendency to maintain its state of rest or uniform motion.
rubric.description: Names inertia.
rubric.how: Use the term inertia.

rubric.why: The car moves forward while the body tends to remain at rest.
rubric.description: Explains the body's tendency when the car accelerates.
rubric.how: State that the body tends to remain at rest as the car moves forward.

modelAnswer: When the car starts moving forward, the body tends to maintain its state of rest.
This tendency is inertia, so the person is pushed back against the seat.
Final answer: The body tends to maintain its state of rest because of inertia.

written.text: The force expressed in Newton's second law is a net force. Why is it so?
written.finalAnswer: Because the acceleration of a body is produced by the resultant force acting on it; balanced forces give zero net force and no acceleration.

rubric.why: Newton’s second law relates acceleration to the total unbalanced force.
rubric.description: Identifies the resultant or net force as the force responsible for acceleration.
rubric.how: State that acceleration is caused by the resultant force.

rubric.why: Balanced forces cancel and therefore do not produce acceleration.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of balanced forces.
rubric.how: State that balanced forces produce zero net force and no acceleration.

modelAnswer: The acceleration of a body is produced by the resultant force acting on it.
Balanced forces cancel, giving zero net force and no acceleration.
Final answer: The force in Newton’s second law is a net force because only the resultant force produces acceleration.

written.text: A horse refuses to pull a cart. The horse argues, “according to Newton's third law, whatever force I exert on the cart, the cart will exert an equal and opposite force on me. Since the net force will be zero, therefore, I have no chance of accelerating (pulling) the cart.” What is wrong with this reasoning?
written.finalAnswer: The horse’s force on the cart and the cart’s reaction force on the horse act on different bodies, so they do not cancel on one body. The ground also exerts a forward frictional force on the horse, which can make the horse and cart accelerate.

rubric.why: Action and reaction forces act on different bodies.
rubric.description: Identifies the two bodies on which the paired forces act.
rubric.how: State that one force acts on the cart and the other on the horse.

rubric.why: Forces on different bodies cannot cancel each other on one body.
rubric.description: Rejects the claim that the two forces make the net force zero.
rubric.how: Explain that the action and reaction do not cancel.

rubric.why: The ground's frictional force on the horse enables forward motion.
rubric.description: Identifies the forward force exerted by the ground.
rubric.how: Mention friction between the horse's feet and the ground.

rubric.why: A non-zero resultant force on the horse-cart system can accelerate it.
rubric.description: Concludes that the horse can pull the cart.
rubric.how: State that the horse and cart can accelerate.

modelAnswer: The horse’s force on the cart and the cart’s reaction force on the horse act on different bodies.
Therefore, these two forces do not cancel each other on one body.
The ground exerts a forward frictional force on the horse.
This force can accelerate the horse and cart.
Final answer: The horse’s reasoning is wrong because action and reaction act on different bodies, and the ground’s forward frictional force can make the horse and cart accelerate.

written.finalAnswer: First law: A body continues its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by some external force. Second law: If a net external force acts upon a body, it accelerates the body in the direction of force; the acceleration is directly proportional to force and inversely proportional to mass, so F = ma. Third law: For every action, there is always an equal and opposite reaction.

rubric.why: The first law describes the motion of a body when no external force changes it.
rubric.description: States Newton’s first law.
rubric.how: Include rest or uniform straight-line motion and the external-force condition.

rubric.why: The second law relates net force to acceleration.
rubric.description: States the second law and its relation.
rubric.how: State that force produces acceleration and write F = ma.

rubric.why: The proportionalities describe how acceleration depends on force and mass.
rubric.description: Includes the force and mass dependence of acceleration.
rubric.how: State that acceleration increases with force and decreases with mass.

rubric.why: The third law describes the paired forces in an interaction.
rubric.description: States Newton’s third law.
rubric.how: State that every action has an equal and opposite reaction.

modelAnswer: Newton’s first law: A body continues its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by some external force.
Newton’s second law: A net external force accelerates a body in the direction of the force; acceleration is directly proportional to force and inversely proportional to mass.
Therefore, F = ma.
Newton’s third law: For every action, there is always an equal and opposite reaction.
Final answer: Newton’s laws are the law of inertia, F = ma for a net force, and the law of equal and opposite action and reaction.

written.text:
A 10 kg block is placed on a smooth horizontal surface. A horizontal force of 5 N is applied to the block. Find:

(a) the acceleration produced in the block.

(b) the velocity of block after 5 seconds.

rubric.why: The second law provides the method for finding acceleration.
rubric.description: Chooses the correct second-law relationship.
rubric.how: Write F = ma or rearrange it as a = F/m.

rubric.why: Substituting the given force and mass gives the acceleration.
rubric.description: Calculates the acceleration correctly.
rubric.how: Substitute F = 5 N and m = 10 kg.

rubric.why: The velocity after the time interval follows from the acceleration.
rubric.description: Uses the equation of motion with the correct initial velocity and time.
rubric.how: Use v = u + at, with u = 0 and t = 5 s.

rubric.why: The final velocity and both requested results must be accurate and include units.
rubric.description: Gives the final acceleration and velocity.
rubric.how: State 0.5 m s⁻² and 2.5 m s⁻¹.

modelAnswer: Given: m = 10 kg, F = 5 N, u = 0, t = 5 s.
(a) F = ma
a = 0.5 m s⁻²
(b) v = u + at
v = 2.5 m s⁻¹
Final answer: (0.5 m s⁻², 2.5 m s⁻¹)

written.text: What force is required to increase the velocity of 800 kg car from 10 m s⁻¹ to 30 m s⁻¹ in 10 seconds?

rubric.why: The acceleration is found from the change in velocity over time.
rubric.description: Finds acceleration from the given velocities and time.
rubric.how: Use a = (v − u)/t.

rubric.why: A correct acceleration is needed before applying the second law.
rubric.description: Calculates acceleration as 2 m s⁻².
rubric.how: Evaluate (30 − 10)/10.

rubric.why: Newton’s second law connects the car’s mass and acceleration to force.
rubric.description: Applies F = ma.
rubric.how: Substitute m = 800 kg and a = 2 m s⁻².

rubric.why: The final force must be correct and expressed in newtons.
rubric.description: Gives the required force.
rubric.how: State 1600 N.

modelAnswer: Given: m = 800 kg, u = 10 m s⁻¹, v = 30 m s⁻¹, t = 10 s.
a = (v − u)/t
F = ma
Final answer: 1600 N

examTips: Short-answer questions often ask for the first law, inertia, or the kinds of velocity change caused by a force. Give the definition clearly and include the key condition.
For a second-law numerical, write F = ma, substitute values with SI units, and show the final answer with the correct unit.
For third-law questions, name both interacting bodies and say the forces are equal and opposite but act on different bodies.
In longer answers about the laws, state each law accurately and include F = ma for the second law.

explain.title: Newton’s first law and inertia
explain.body: Your textbook states: “A body continues its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by some external force.” This means an object does not change its motion by itself. The property of a body to maintain its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line is called inertia. Mass measures inertia: a greater mass means greater inertia.

explain.title: Newton’s second law
explain.body: Your textbook states that if a net external force acts on a body, it accelerates in the direction of the force. Acceleration is directly proportional to force and inversely proportional to mass. The relation is F = ma. One newton produces an acceleration of 1 m s⁻² in a body of mass 1 kg.

explain.title: Force changes velocity
explain.body: A force can produce acceleration or deceleration and so change velocity. Because velocity is a vector, the change may be in its magnitude, direction, or both.

explain.title: Newton’s third law
explain.body: Your textbook states: “For every action, there is always an equal and opposite reaction.” The two forces act on different bodies, so they do not balance each other. For example, when a gun fires a bullet forward, the gun recoils backward.

mistakes: Do not say that action and reaction cancel each other; they act on different bodies.
Use the net or resultant force in F = ma, not just one force when other forces also act.
Do not confuse inertia with force; inertia is a property of a body and depends on its mass.
When using F = ma, write the units: force in newtons, mass in kilograms, and acceleration in m s⁻².
Do not claim that a force can only change speed; it can change direction too.
